chain.label: Night flight in dark cockpit conditions
chain.trigger: The accident occurred at night in dark lighting conditions.

chain.label: Relief first officer presses for an unusually early transfer of control
chain.trigger: About 20 minutes after takeoff (about 0140), the relief first officer suggested that he relieve the command first officer... A transfer of control this early in the flight was contrary to the EgyptAir practice

chain.label: Relief first officer alone at the controls after the captain left the cockpit
chain.trigger: the evidence indicates that the relief first officer was alone in the cockpit from about 0148:19, when the command captain left the cockpit, to 0150:06, when he returned

caused_by.evidence: the command first officer vacated and the relief first officer moved into the first officer's seat

chain.label: Autopilot manually disconnected in cruise with no operational reason
chain.trigger: Because the relief first officer was alone in the cockpit, the evidence indicates that he manually disconnected the autopilot... there was no logical operational reason for the relief first officer to disconnect the autopilot while in cruise flight over the ocean

caused_by.evidence: all manual flight control inputs made after 0148:19, until the command captain's return to the cockpit at 0150:06, must have been made by the relief first officer

chain.label: Relief first officer retards throttles to idle and commands sustained nose-down elevator
chain.trigger: At 0149:53, the throttle levers were moved from their cruise power setting to idle, and, at 0149:54, the FDR recorded an abrupt nose-down elevator movement

caused_by.evidence: it is apparent that the throttle lever movements at 0149:53 were caused by the relief first officer's manual inputs and were not the result of autothrottle commands
the airplane remained essentially in level flight about FL 330 for about 8 seconds after the autopilot was disconnected

chain.label: Airplane departs cruise into a steep dive exceeding maximum operating airspeed
chain.trigger: the airplane began to rapidly pitch nose down and descend... at 0150:08, as the airplane exceeded its maximum operating airspeed (0.86 Mach), a master warning alarm began to sound

caused_by.evidence: the nose-down elevator movements were not the result of a failure in the elevator control system or any other airplane system but were the result of the relief first officer's manipulation of the airplane controls

chain.label: Opposing control column inputs after the captain returns; elevator surfaces split
chain.trigger: the elevator surfaces remained in a split condition (with the left surface commanding nose up and the right surface commanding nose down) until the FDR and CVR stopped recording

caused_by.evidence: opposing pilot inputs where the relief first officer was commanding nose-down and the captain was commanding nose-up movement
the CVR recorded the sounds of the captain asking loudly... 'What's happening? What's happening?,' as he returned to the cockpit
The visual difference between pushing forward on the control column and pulling aft... would not have been readily apparent to the captain in the darkened cockpit

chain.label: Both engines shut down when start levers moved to cutoff
chain.trigger: The FDR data indicated that the engine start lever switches for both engines moved from the run to the cutoff position between 0150:21 and 0150:23.

caused_by.evidence: the evidence indicates that the relief first officer moved the engine start lever switches to the cutoff position (a counterproductive action, in terms of recovery)
After the elevator split began, the relief first officer shut down the engines.

chain.label: Recovery not accomplished; airplane climbs, then enters a second rapid descent
chain.trigger: However, a successful recovery—although possible—was not accomplished... the airplane began a second rapid descent that continued until it impacted the ocean

caused_by.evidence: The captain's failure to recover the airplane can be explained, in part, by the relief first officer's opposing flight control inputs.
It is possible that efforts to recover the airplane after the airplane lost electrical power were also complicated by the loss of electronic cockpit displays.

chain.label: High-speed impact with the Atlantic Ocean
chain.trigger: the data indicate that the airplane impacted the ocean about 0152:30, with an average descent rate during the second dive of about 20,000 fpm

caused_by.evidence: the airplane began a second rapid descent that continued until it impacted the ocean

chain.label: All 217 occupants killed and airplane destroyed
chain.trigger: All 217 people on board were killed, and the airplane was destroyed.

caused_by.evidence: The small size of most of the recovered pieces of wreckage was consistent with the airplane impacting the water at a high speed.
